en: Permissions are an important topic when
working with Claude Code, so I have to get
back to those because we already saw that
Claude Code asks for permissions from time
to time. For example, it asks for
permissions before it starts editing files.
At least it does that if you send your
prompt in the normal default mode you get
out of the box. So for example, if I were to
send this prompt in a new session without
any other changes, also no changes in my
settings, Then after evaluating my prompt,
Claude will ask me for permission to edit
this page.tsx file, also by showing me the
changes it wants to perform. So as before, I
can choose yes to grant this permission once
and be asked again if it wants to edit
another file or choose the second option or
hit Shift+Tab if I want to permanently grant
this permission. And with Escape, I can
cancel this edit and this entire session
actually, and I could send up follow-up
messages to continue it. Of course, it's
quite likely that you want to allow Claude
Code to edit your files and you don't want
to wait for it to ask you for permission
because you wanna go grab a coffee right
away.
You can therefore switch the mode from the
default mode by hitting Shift+Tab to switch
to this Accept Edits mode here. And that
does just what the name implies. It will
automatically accept file edits inside of
your project. Claude Code still can't access
anything else on your system. We're talking
about files in your project.
The same prompt in this mode, it will do the
same research, come to the same conclusion
probably, but it will then edit the file
without asking me first.
As you see here, I did not have to grant it
permissions. However, it's important to
understand that even in this mode, it still
is not allowed to do everything. It's just
allowed to edit your code files. But what if
I ask it to create a new Git commit about
these changes it made because I'm too lazy
to type out the Git commit message myself?
As you'll see, it uses the bash tool here a
couple of times to
check the current status and find out what
happened in the past and what changed so
that it can craft a proper commit message.
But then when it wants to run git add, which
of course is a command that changes
something,
and also then git commit to commit that
snapshot,
it does ask for permission again because by
default, Claude Code is configured to not be
allowed to do everything even in this accept
edits mode because now we're not editing a
file in this project. Instead, here we're
creating a git commit. And the same would be
true if it, for example, wanted to create a
new folder or do anything else that's not
just editing a code file.
So in that case, you still have to make a
choice and you can either allow this one
time or in general tell it to not ask again
for git add and git commit commands, which
means it will still come back to you if it
wants to use some other command that changes
something like git restore or other bash
commands. But for these commands, it won't
ask again. And here I'll just accept this,
this one time because I wanna get asked
again in the future, let's say. So it's
important to understand how it handles
permission and that even this accept edits
mode does not allow everything. But let's
say you really wanna be able to move away
from your machine and let Claude Code do its
thing without it ever asking for any
permissions. If that is what you want, you
can start a new Claude session by adding the
--dangerously-skip-permissions flag. And
that does just what it sounds like. It skips
all
permission requests. It will always grant
those permissions Claude code wants.
And it's dangerous because of course
you then got no control over what it does.
It still can't access your hard drive
outside of your project, but it can can
erase your Git history, erase files that
can't be brought back in this project. It
could write a script that then is able to do
something outside of your project. If it
writes a bash script that erases your hard
drive and it executes that in your project,
then this should work and should destroy
your machine.
Obviously, that's not necessarily super
likely to happen, but it could happen.
And that's why you should use this flag with
care.
But you can of course use it. You then get a
warning what this does and you can then
accept that you are aware of that. And then
I could send a prompt like this where I ask
it to edit something and also commit the
changes.
And then I could leave and come back once
it's done and it will never ask for any
permissions.
So as you see, it edited the file without
asking for permission
and it created that commit.
